vignette: Miguel is a 24-year-old Latin American male who works as a QA Engineer. Miguel's life was upended when he survived a catastrophic explosion at his former workplace. Since then, everyday experiences have become intensely triggering for him. Conversations about accidents send waves of anxiety through him, and he often finds himself dissociating from reality, feeling like an observer in his own life. Even watching the news can be overwhelming, with reports of similar incidents evoking a visceral fear that seems to paralyze him. Miguel's distress has driven him to adopt various maladaptive strategies as coping mechanisms. He frequently engages in counterfactual thinking, ruminating on how different his life would have been if he had managed to prevent the disaster. This line of thought is often triggered by discussions about accidents and news reports that remind him of the incident. Each time he hears such talk or sees a related story, he becomes entrenched in thoughts of what could have been done differently. Miguel's negative appraisals are deeply rooted in his sense of failure and fear. He feels an intense guilt for not being able to protect others during the explosion. This belief that he should have done more is particularly potent when triggered by conversations or news related to such disasters. The feeling of detachment further exacerbates these thoughts, making him question whether he can ever trust himself again. These negative appraisals also fuel his maladaptive strategies. Miguel’s conviction that he failed to protect others and his fear that harm could come from any unexpected source have made it difficult for him to move forward. He avoids watching TV programs or reading about similar events because they reinforce his belief that nothing good can happen to him anymore, and that he will inevitably fail in protecting himself and others. Miguel’s avoidance of the police is another manifestation of these maladaptive strategies. The explosion was a traumatic event that involved a man-made disaster, and encountering figures of authority like the police only intensifies his fear and guilt. This avoidance has started to impact his daily life; he often misses important meetings or deadlines at work because he feels too overwhelmed to leave his home. The cumulative effect of these strategies and beliefs is a cycle that seems to tighten around Miguel’s daily existence. Each trigger reinforces his negative appraisals, leading him deeper into counterfactual thinking and avoidance behaviors. This has left Miguel feeling increasingly isolated and hopeless about the future. What finally pushed Miguel to seek help was a particularly triggering conversation at work about an accident in another company. The dissociative feelings and overwhelming anxiety were so intense that he realized he could no longer function effectively without intervention. Miguel is most afraid of being unable to protect others again, but he also hopes for a way to break free from the cycle of guilt and fear that has consumed his life. In therapy, Miguel will need to explore these triggers, negative appraisals, and maladaptive strategies in depth. He hopes to find ways to process his traumatic experience and regain a sense of control over his thoughts and actions.
